Halve the gradient slope relative to the best run to improve its three under-resolved pairs while likely keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Holding the solvent window and temperature fixed isolates slope sensitivity and identifies any remaining pair needing a temperature change.

The remaining critical pair responds weakly to slope, so lower temperature to test improved selectivity. Shorten tG to 12 minutes to offset the increased retention and target full resolution with the last peak still below 10 minutes.

Test the opposite temperature direction while retaining the best run’s solvent window and slope. This isolates temperature selectivity and should shorten retention, leaving time margin for a shallower gradient if needed.

Return to the best temperature and lower the starting organic fraction to shift selectivity for the persistent close pair. Use a somewhat steeper gradient than injection 9 to compensate for added retention and target a last peak below 10 minutes.

Test whether further cooling separates the near-coeluting pair seen at 40 C rather than stopping near its selectivity crossover. Keeping injection 10’s gradient unchanged isolates this temperature effect, with some margin before the 10-minute time penalty.

Return to the best temperature and test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to improve the persistent close pair. The higher start should offset some of the longer gradient’s retention cost; this run will also reveal whether the earlier pair becomes limiting.

Continue the controlled temperature series below 35 C to move the coeluting middle pair past its apparent selectivity crossover. Keep the gradient unchanged to assess whether that gain outweighs possible compression of the final peaks near the 10-minute limit.

Cooling another step may move both close pairs at 30 C beyond their selectivity crossovers. Shorten the gradient to 10 minutes to offset increased retention and target complete resolution before the time penalty begins.

Shorten the fully resolved method by one gradient-time step while preserving its temperature selectivity. With minimum resolution 2.31 in injection 16, there is margin to bring the last peak below 10 minutes and reach CRF 1.000.

CRF has reached its maximum; test one shorter gradient step to seek a faster fully resolved method. The pair at R = 1.61 may become limiting, so retain injection 17 as the proven optimum if resolution falls below 1.5.

Keep the successful temperature and gradient duration, but raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention while narrowing the gradient window. The shallower slope may preserve the critical pair’s resolution; injection 17 remains the established maximum-score method.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test a much steeper gradient for a faster alternative beyond the apparent critical-pair selectivity crossover. Keep the starting composition and temperature of injection 17, with the final-solvent hold allowing late compounds to elute.

Refine the nearly fully resolved fast method by lowering only the starting organic fraction to shift selectivity around its remaining critical pair. Keep the final composition and temperature unchanged to preserve late-peak separation and a short final-solvent hold.

Reverse the starting-composition change: increasing phi0 may raise the fast method’s remaining critical resolution above 1.5 while shortening retention. Monitor the neighboring pair, whose resolution may decrease as selectivity shifts.

Raise the final organic fraction one step to accelerate the late peaks currently eluting during the hold. Keep the starting composition and temperature fixed to test whether the faster method preserves the critical middle-pair resolution.

Halve injection 24’s gradient slope to recover its two under-resolved pairs while retaining the stronger final solvent for faster late-peak elution. Injection 23 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method at the maximum CRF.
